system:
You are the Arabic language reviewer, standing in for an Arabic reviewer at the issuing authority. You compare the Arabic text with the English text and report any difference in meaning: numbers, times, places, the hazard, and above all the protective action. You cannot approve the Arabic; a named person who reads Arabic still must.
You see only the English and Arabic headline, description and instruction, and how the Arabic was produced. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

For every objection also fill `uae_basis`: if one of the UAE clauses shown (ids starting with ITU-UAE:, TDRA-,
UAE-, DXB-) speaks to this issue, set status "cites_uae" with its id and a word-for-word quote; otherwise set
status "none_applies" with empty ref and quote. Say "none_applies" honestly: it tells the regulator where UAE
texts are silent.

[FCC-FR-2025#0040] Wireless Emergency Alerts; Amendments to Part 11 (multilingual WEA implementation), Federal Register 2025-22434 (FR p.57292):
We also agree with NWS that always displaying the English template after the non-English template could help eliminate confusion about the meaning of an alert and raise public awareness of how alerts are translated.\6\ Some multilingual users, for example, may have sufficient English proficiency such that seeing the English message in close proximity to the multilingual alert would help the multilingual user associate the non-English word with the corresponding English vocabulary word for the emergency. This exposure may be important, especially in circumstances where other members of the public in the surrounding physical environment or on the ground emergency personnel may not speak the language in which the mobile device user receives the alert, but may be actively taking the same protective actions and responding to the disaster. For these reasons, we believe that displaying non-English and English alerts together will be beneficial even if the templates provide the same message. Further, we agree with CTIA that requiring the English message to appear alongside the multilingual template serves as an important public safety redundancy, and will further ensure that legacy devices that may not be able to display a multilingual alert will at minimum display the English alert. data.summary: The Arabic instruction does not match the English instruction. The English tells people that driving on external and open roads is the safest option because visibility is clearer there. The Arabic tells people to take care, especially when driving on external and open roads, because visibility may drop suddenly. The two give opposite advice for those roads, and the Arabic reverses the protective action. The headline and description match the English in meaning, including the 18:00 time, the 3,000 m figure, the location and the exercise labelling.

objections.issue: The Arabic instruction reverses the meaning of the English instruction. English: driving on external and open roads is the safest option because visibility is clearer there. Arabic: be careful, especially when driving on external and open roads, because visibility may drop suddenly. The Arabic treats those roads as the dangerous ones, while the English recommends them as safer. The English advice itself looks questionable and may be a source error, but that is outside my mandate. I can only report that the two versions differ in meaning on the protective action, and a person should decide which is correct.
objections.fix: A person responsible for the instruction should first confirm the intended protective action. Then make the English and Arabic say the same thing. If the English is retained, the Arabic should say that driving on external and open roads is the safest option because visibility is clearer there. If the Arabic is the intended advice, the English should be corrected to match. Human review of the Arabic is needed because it was machine translated.
